title: Conversation memory and summaries
subtitle: The model remembers nothing: you choose what to resend with each message
mission: Aurinha helps a customer over eight messages and, at the end, he asks about something he said at the start. Choose how to build memory (none, window, summary or everything) and find the point where she forgets, without wasting tokens.

predict.question: sending the summary of the start plus the last 2 messages, instead of the whole conversation, costs…

options.less: Far fewer tokens: the summary fits in a few lines
options.same: The same: the summary repeats everything
options.more: More: the summary adds on top of the history

feedback.right: right: the summary swaps six messages for two lines and only the last two stay verbatim. That’s why summarizing allows long conversations without overflowing the context window.
feedback.wrong: it costs far fewer: the summary replaces the old messages (it doesn’t add to them) and only the last two stay verbatim. Compare the savings in the scene.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Run with summary and then with the full conversation and compare tokens.

why.simples:
A language model remembers nothing between one message and the next: with every question, the system has to resend the conversation. It’s like talking to someone who forgets everything every five minutes, and you hand over a note with what matters before each sentence.
There are three ways to write the note: send everything (expensive), only the latest messages (cheap, but forgets the start) or a summary of the start plus the latest messages.
why.dev:
Anthropic’s Messages API and OpenAI’s Chat Completions keep no state: every request carries the whole history, which counts tokens and fills the context window (some APIs keep the history on the server, like OpenAI’s Responses API, but it still counts tokens on every call). Common strategies: sliding window (last N messages), a summary of old messages (made by the model itself) plus the recent ones, and fixed facts pulled into a separate block (order, preferences).
Sending too much context isn’t free either: Anthropic’s docs note that accuracy and recall degrade as context grows ("context rot") and that curating what goes in matters as much as the space available. Some providers offer automatic server-side compaction (in the Anthropic API, in beta when this was written, Nov 2026).
why.especialista:
A summary is lossy: what doesn’t make it in stops existing for the model, and an error in the summary becomes a "fact". Protect what must not be forgotten by keeping structured fields (order number, consents, decisions) outside the summary and always reinjecting them. Summarize on a trigger (past X tokens), keep recent messages verbatim and log which summary was used, so you can reproduce a bad answer later.
Memory across conversations is another problem, with privacy (LGPD): keep only what’s needed, with consent and an expiry, and let the person see and delete it. Measure with questions that go back to the start of the conversation, like this lesson, and not just by how fluent the answer is.

ui: Pick a question and the memory strategy.

Memory "window" with the order number question.

--memory none, window, summary or full; --recent 1 to 8.

steps: Build a test conversation of 10 messages where the customer gives 3 pieces of information (order, preference, address) at different moments.
At the end, ask about each piece with three memories: only the last 4 messages, an LLM-made summary plus the last 4, and the whole conversation. Count the tokens sent in each.
Note what the summary left out and move those fields into a fixed block that is always resent.
recipe.ok: only the last 4 forgets the information from the start, the summary keeps part of it and costs far less than the whole conversation, and with the fixed block all 3 pieces come back.
